results.name: round_target_yes_no_round_examples
results.description: Yes rate for targets that are multiples of 10, among sets containing no multiple of 10; observed above null means people favour round-number targets (a round-number bias the model lacks), below means the model over-endorses them.
results.code:
# name: round_target_yes_no_round_examples
# description: Yes rate for targets that are multiples of 10, among sets containing no multiple of 10; observed above null means people favour round-number targets (a round-number bias the model lacks), below means the model over-endorses them.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    parsed = {s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")] for s in uniq}
    ex = np.full((len(df), 4), np.nan)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    table = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = parsed[s][:4]
        table[i, :len(v)] = v
    ex = table[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    any_round = np.any(np.mod(ex, 10) == 0, axis=1)
    m = ~any_round & (np.mod(t, 10) == 0)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: single_example_near_minus_far_yes
results.description: On single-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed above null means people's one-shot generalisation is more similarity/proximity-graded than the model predicts (model too rule-driven), below means the model overweights proximity.
results.code:
# name: single_example_near_minus_far_yes
# description: On single-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed above null means people's one-shot generalisation is more similarity/proximity-graded than the model predicts (model too rule-driven), below means the model overweights proximity.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single), errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.abs(t - x)
    near = single.to_numpy() & (d > 0) & (d <= 10)
    far = single.to_numpy() & (d > 30)
    if not near.any() or not far.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[near].mean() - y[far].mean())

results.name: inside_minus_outside_range_yes
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets strictly inside the examples' [min, max] span minus the yes rate for targets outside it, among sets of 2+ examples; observed above null means people treat the example span as a sharper boundary than the (centre-weighted) model predicts, below means people extend past the extremes even more than the model.
results.code:
# name: inside_minus_outside_range_yes
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets strictly inside the examples' [min, max] span minus the yes rate for targets outside it, among sets of 2+ examples; observed above null means people treat the example span as a sharper boundary than the (centre-weighted) model predicts, below means people extend past the extremes even more than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    parsed = {s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")] for s in uniq}
    ex = np.full((len(df), 4), np.nan)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    table = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = parsed[s][:4]
        table[i, :len(v)] = v
    ex = table[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~is_ex
    ins = base & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    out = base & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if not ins.any() or not out.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[ins].mean() - y[out].mean())

results.name: trial_index_yes_drift
results.description: Yes rate in the second half of the session (trial_index >= 225) minus the first half; a nonzero observed value relative to null means people's yes bias drifts over the session (positive: more liberal later, negative: more conservative later), which the stationary model cannot produce beyond stimulus-order differences.

results.name: mixed_ending_units_digit_match_yes
results.description: Yes rate for targets whose units digit matches at least one example's units digit (target not itself an example), among multi-example sets whose examples do NOT all share one units digit; observed above null means people generalise by digit similarity that the model's single-digit rules cannot express (model under-produces), below means the reverse.
results.code:
# name: mixed_ending_units_digit_match_yes
# description: Yes rate for targets whose units digit matches at least one example's units digit (target not itself an example), among multi-example sets whose examples do NOT all share one units digit; observed above null means people generalise by digit similarity that the model's single-digit rules cannot express (model under-produces), below means the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    parsed = {s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")] for s in uniq}
    ex = np.full((len(df), 4), np.nan)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    table = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = parsed[s][:4]
        table[i, :len(v)] = v
    ex = table[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    u = np.mod(ex, 10)
    same_end = np.nanmax(u, axis=1) == np.nanmin(u, axis=1)
    match = np.any(u == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & ~same_end & match & ~is_ex
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: set_size_yes_contrast
results.description: Overall yes rate on 4-example sets minus yes rate on 2-example sets; observed more negative than null means people narrow their generalisation with more examples more strongly than the model's size principle predicts, more positive means the model narrows too fast.

results.name: lag1_response_repetition
results.description: Proportion of consecutive trials (adjacent rows, trial_index differing by 1, same number_set) on which the response repeats the previous response; observed above null means sequential perseveration/response inertia the stateless model does not produce, below means excess alternation.

results.name: opposite_parity_near_target_yes
results.description: Yes rate for targets of the opposite parity to the examples lying within 5 of some example, among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity; observed above null means people generalise by numeric proximity even against a parity regularity more than the model predicts (model too rule-bound), below means the model over-generalises across parity.
results.code:
# name: opposite_parity_near_target_yes
# description: Yes rate for targets of the opposite parity to the examples lying within 5 of some example, among sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity; observed above null means people generalise by numeric proximity even against a parity regularity more than the model predicts (model too rule-bound), below means the model over-generalises across parity.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    parsed = {s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")] for s in uniq}
    ex = np.full((len(df), 4), np.nan)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    table = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = parsed[s][:4]
        table[i, :len(v)] = v
    ex = table[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    p = np.mod(ex, 2)
    same_par = (np.nanmax(p, axis=1) == np.nanmin(p, axis=1))
    opp = np.mod(t, 2) != np.nanmax(p, axis=1)
    near = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1) <= 5
    m = (n >= 2) & same_par & opp & near
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
